enrichment.short_title: Shopping centre fit-out floor damage — breach found but causation fails on mall water ingress
key_facts: Woolworths carried out tenant fit-out works at Store C, Friars Square shopping centre, Aylesbury, in September 1992 before an intended opening; Amtico floor adhesive failed on 21–22 September 1992.
Henry Boot Management Ltd (HBM) was management contractor for Friends Provident's redevelopment; Woolworths sued HBM in negligence for water-related damage to the floor screed.

Woolworths alleged flooding of adjacent Unit 21 and migration of water through an internal wall caused the failure; HBM contended the dominant cause was rainwater from the open mall/atrium entering via the unprotected screed edge at shop frontages.
Quantum was agreed at £123,119 if liability were established; Woolworths discontinued its claim against FP on agreed costs terms.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in Technology and Construction Court on negligence claim following discontinued claim against second defendant.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; although HBM was in breach of duty, Woolworths failed to prove that breach caused the adhesive failure.
enrichment.ratio: A management contractor owed Woolworths a concurrent tort duty after handover to exercise reasonable skill and care with due regard to the tenant's interests, including protecting an internal wall in Unit 21 from rainwater accumulation; however, where adhesive failure occurred uniformly across the shop front and mall-sourced water via the unprotected screed edge was the effective cause, breach as to Unit 21 water ingress was not causative and the claim fails.
legal_issues: Whether HBM owed Woolworths a common law duty of care after handover of Store C
Whether HBM was in breach in failing to protect the internal wall and Unit 21 from rainwater
Whether breach or water from Unit 21, as opposed to mall/atrium ingress at the screed edge, caused the floor failure
Quantum and betterment if liability had been established
Whether late re-amendment of particulars should be permitted

enrichment.short_title: Insurers' loss adjuster knowledge attributed in subrogated s.14A limitation claim
key_facts: Claimant's bungalow subsidence recurred after underpinning works advised by Entec completed in August 1992; insurers (Sun Alliance) paid and later sued Entec in the claimant's name by subrogation for wasted remedial costs.
Proceedings issued July 2000; first instance judge held the claim time-barred under section 14A because insurer-appointed loss adjuster Mr Handford had requisite knowledge by November 1996.
Experts appointed by the loss adjuster concluded from late 1996 that oak trees and inadequate underpinning explained continuing movement, but Mr Turner's final report was not until July 1997.
Claimant personally lacked knowledge until the Turner report, but the judge imputed the loss adjuster's knowledge to the insurers and thus the nominal claimant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from preliminary issue trial on whether negligent geotechnical advice claim was time-barred under section 14A Limitation Act 1980.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; claim held time-barred.
enrichment.ratio: In a subrogated action the relevant knowledge for section 14A(5) is that of the person with the real interest in pursuing the claim—the insurer—and knowledge acquired by an independent loss adjuster investigating the claim on the insurer's behalf is attributable to the insurer; an experienced loss adjuster may have actual knowledge before a final expert report is delivered where interim expert findings already establish the material facts.
legal_issues: Whether a loss adjuster's knowledge is attributable to the claimant in a subrogated claim
Whether insurers' knowledge fixes the nominal plaintiff under section 14A(5)
Whether a claimant must wait for a final expert report before limitation time starts under section 14A(10)
When Mr Handford acquired knowledge of causation and defendant identity

enrichment.short_title: Head-tenant break notice terminates subleases despite contractual 'subject to underleases' clause
key_facts: PW held a head lease of a London office building from CLRP/Milton Gate; it granted seven underleases to BT group companies on the shared misconception that subtenancies would survive exercise of a head-tenant break notice.
Headlease clause 5(6) allowed PW to determine on 24 June 2002 by 12 months' notice 'subject to any Permitted Underleases' and required payment of a nine-month rent penalty.
PW served the break notice; parties had understood since Brown v Wilson that subleases would continue, but Pennell v Payne and Barrett v Morgan established the opposite at common law.
Milton Gate acquired the reversion, negotiated with BT for an overriding lease, then relied on strict legal termination; BT accepted subleases ended; PW became liable for the penalty.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of connected claims between head-tenant PW, landlord Milton Gate and subtenants BT on effect of break notice and estoppel.
enrichment.outcome: Underleases held to have expired on 24 June 2002; PW liable to pay the contractual penalty to Milton Gate; no operative estoppel by convention between any party.
enrichment.ratio: Parties cannot contract out of the rule in Pennell v Payne that a subtenancy determined when the head tenancy is validly determined by break notice; a break clause cannot be recharacterised as a surrender provision; although a convention arose that subleases would survive, mutual resiling and BT's acceptance of termination prevented estoppel by convention from altering the strict legal outcome.
legal_issues: Whether clause 5(6) could preserve subtenancies on head-lease break
Whether Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995 sections 139/141 or Human Rights Act 1998 section 3 altered enforceability of sublease covenants
Whether break notice could be treated as surrender
Estoppel by deed and estoppel by convention in a tripartite landlord/head-tenant/subtenant context
Whether Milton Gate and BT mutually resiled from the convention

enrichment.short_title: Section 152 ASB injunctions unavailable to protect owner-occupiers near council housing
key_facts: Two linked appeals concerned anti-social behaviour injunctions under section 152 Housing Act 1996 with powers of arrest against youths G (Wigan) and Lee (Manchester).
In each case the primary complainant (Mr McDonough and Mr Andrew) was an owner-occupier living near, but not in, secure local authority residential premises.
County court judges had granted or sought to reinstate 'usual form' injunctions protecting persons in the locality of council housing.
Court of Appeal held binding authority in Enfield LBC v B and Nottingham City Council v Thames required a nexus between protected persons or their activities and identifiable LA residential premises.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals against county court decisions on applications for section 152 anti-social behaviour injunctions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in Wigan case (injunction set aside); appeal dismissed in Manchester case (refusal to reinstate upheld); applications to appeal to House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 152(1)(a) does not protect persons simply residing in the locality of local authority residential premises; there must be a connection or nexus between the protected person's residence, visit or lawful activity and identifiable residential premises to which the section applies; owner-occupiers near an estate are outside the section, and broadly framed 'usual form' injunctions exceed the statutory power.
legal_issues: Construction of 'in the locality of such premises' in section 152(1)(a)
Whether Enfield and Nottingham bindingly require a nexus test
Whether proximity of owner-occupiers or estate-wide conduct suffices
Appropriate form and proportionality of section 152 injunctions
Effect of pending Anti-social Behaviour Bill reforms

enrichment.short_title: Permission refused on disability discrimination dismissal — no error of law
key_facts: Mr Tuckett, a principal consultant at Ovum Ltd, was dismissed in March 2000 for under-performance after less than 12 months' service; he could not bring ordinary unfair dismissal claim.
Employment Tribunal found he was disabled (depressive/bipolar illness) but not dismissed for a reason relating to his disability; breach of contract and wages claims also failed.
Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissed his appeal on a preliminary hearing as having no reasonable prospect of success on the law.
He applied out of time for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal, citing illness, mistaken belief that review was the correct route, and wished to adduce later psychiatric evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal and extension of time against EAT decision dismissing disability discrimination appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Applications for permission to appeal and extension of time refused.
enrichment.ratio: The Court of Appeal may intervene only on questions of law, not to retry factual findings; where the employment tribunal correctly directed itself on disability discrimination law and found dismissal was for under-performance unrelated to disability, there is no appealable error even if the applicant is aggrieved, and delay of over a year without exceptional circumstances does not warrant extension.
legal_issues: Whether ET erred in law in finding dismissal not for reason related to disability
Whether tribunal should have adopted a proactive approach in mental disability cases
Admissibility of additional medical evidence on appeal
Whether extension of time should be granted for late appeal

enrichment.short_title: No security for costs under Insolvency Rule 4.120 where removal claim is arguable
key_facts: Quicksons, parent of Buildlead Ltd in creditors' voluntary liquidation, applied to remove liquidators Katz and Kelmanson under section 108(2) Insolvency Act 1986.

Liquidators sought £59,750 security for their defence costs under Insolvency Rule 4.120(3), triggered by Quicksons' section 236 information application about August 1997 transfers to Quicksons' bank account.
Quicksons alleged prolonged liquidation and partiality; liquidators accepted the removal claim was arguable though disputed on merits.
Quicksons was solvent with sufficient cash to pay any security sought.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application for security for costs in section 108 liquidator removal proceedings.
enrichment.ratio: Insolvency Rule 4.120(3) is best construed as a merits-based filter at the first stage under rule 4.120(2), analogous to conditional permission to defend under CPR Part 24, rather than a general security provision parallel to CPR 25.13; where the applicant shows sufficient cause and the removal claim is arguable, security should not be ordered.
legal_issues: Proper construction and purpose of Insolvency Rule 4.120(3)
Whether discretion is security-based or merits-based
Relationship between Insolvency Rules and CPR Parts 24 and 25
Whether Quicksons' removal claim disclosed sufficient cause

enrichment.short_title: CAC erred in disregarding union members' objection letters on statutory recognition

statutes_considered.title: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992

key_facts: TSSA applied to the Central Arbitration Committee for recognition at Gatwick Express for a defined bargaining unit of 38 managerial staff, of whom 20 were union members.
Paragraph 22(2)(b) was satisfied by membership majority, but paragraph 22(4)(b) required a secret ballot if a significant number of union members in the unit objected.
Eight union members signed standard-form letters opposing recognition; seven were forwarded via Gatwick Express HR and one sent direct to the CAC.
The CAC panel gave the letters no evidential weight, finding they had not been 'received' and doubting validity because members had not resigned from the union.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review (permission granted and treated as substantive hearing) of CAC union recognition decision.
enrichment.outcome: CAC decision quashed; CAC ordered to give notice of intention to hold a secret ballot pursuant to agreed terms between Gatwick Express and TSSA.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 22(4)(b) is not limited to direct written notification from workers to the CAC; where eight of twenty union members objected (40%), that is a significant number triggering the mandatory ballot procedure, and it was irrational to treat letters before the panel as unreceived or irrelevant because they passed through the employer.
legal_issues: Construction of 'inform the CAC' in paragraph 22(4)(b)
Whether employer-channelled objection letters are valid evidence
Whether eight of twenty objectors is a significant number
Whether court may direct CAC to arrange ballot or must remit for fresh decision
Appropriate remedy where claimant and union agree on outcome

enrichment.short_title: Wednesbury unreasonable medical assessment refusing emergency housing transfer for asthma
key_facts: Claimant Maryan Maali, a secured tenant in a third-floor maisonette without a lift with four young children, applied to Lambeth for a transfer from January 2001 citing severe asthma.
GP letters supported that climbing stairs when asthma was bad was impossible or very difficult and ground-floor accommodation would benefit her health.
Lambeth's allocation scheme was conceded unlawful following R (A and Lindsay) v Lambeth; a compliant scheme was not due until February 2004.

Medical adviser Barbara Stones' assessment of 8 August 2003 refused Group B emergency listing, attributing stays with a friend to childcare needs and treating stair-climbing as beneficial exercise for asthma control.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Lambeth housing allocation scheme and medical assessment for transfer priority.
enrichment.outcome: 8 August assessment quashed; mandatory order for re-assessment for Group B within 28 days; wider declarations and mandatory order to assess under section 167(2) refused; claimant awarded costs.
enrichment.ratio: A housing medical adviser's refusal of emergency transfer priority was Wednesbury unreasonable where she failed to address the GP-supported inability to climb stairs when asthma was severe and substituted an unsupported childcare explanation, and irrationally treated stair-climbing as therapeutically equivalent to prescribed breathing exercises while ignoring carrying children and shopping; however, where no lawful allocation scheme exists and an interim section 167(2) assessment is impracticable, the court will grant only limited Group B re-assessment relief.
legal_issues: Whether 8 August medical assessment complied with Group B emergency criteria
Whether Barbara Stones was a suitable decision-maker
Whether assessment was Wednesbury unreasonable
Whether mandatory order should require assessment under section 167(2)
Whether wider declarations on scheme unlawfulness should be granted

enrichment.short_title: Section 37/41 hospital order quashed where defendant unfit to plead — no Article 5 breach

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Procedure (Insanity and Unfitness to Plead) Act 1991

key_facts: Claimant A was found unfit to plead and a jury found he did the act charged on count 2 (assault occasioning ABH) but not counts 1 or 3.
On 11 September 2002 the Crown Court, apparently unaware of the unfitness findings, made a section 37 hospital order with section 41 restrictions under the Mental Health Act 1983.
A was detained at Three Bridges Unit and later became an informal patient after clinicians found section 3 criteria were not met.
Damages claim was abandoned; judicial review sought quashing of the order, correction of records and declaration of Article 5 infringement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Crown Court hospital/restriction order made after insanity Act findings.
enrichment.outcome: Hospital order quashed; records to be corrected; no Article 5 violation; court to reconstitute as Crown Court to make lawful section 5(2) 1964 Act order if appropriate.
enrichment.ratio: A section 37 MHA order requires a conviction and is unavailable where a jury has found unfitness to plead and only that the defendant did the act charged; the correct power is a section 5(2) Criminal Procedure (Insanity) Act 1964 admission order, but an irregular Crown Court order remains legally effective until set aside so consequent detention was lawful under domestic law and not arbitrary for Article 5.1(e) purposes.
legal_issues: Whether section 37/41 MHA order could be made without conviction after insanity Act findings
Appropriate remedy by judicial review
Whether detention was 'in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law' under Article 5
Whether detention was lawful and non-arbitrary under Article 5.1(e)
Effect of quashing on continuing detention authority

key_facts: Algerian citizen Mr Khalfi claimed asylum in June 1997 citing threats from the GIA; special adjudicator dismissed his appeal in September 2000 after a hearing in his absence.
